findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() does not return BouncyCastle
findings.body: Despite its name, `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns the Provider that backs the JVM's default keystore type (typically SUN or SunJSSE), not BouncyCastle: `return KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider();`. This is a deliberate workaround because the authz-client module does not depend on BouncyCastle, but the method name promises a BC Provider. Any caller that selects algorithms specific to BouncyCastle (e.g. certain EC curves, RSA-PSS variants, JOSE algorithms only BC exposes) will silently get the JCA default provider and may behave unexpectedly. The misleading contract should at least be renamed (e.g. `getDefaultProvider()`), or the method should throw UnsupportedOperationException to be consistent with the rest of this class.

findings.title: Dead ASN1Encoder invocations in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
readSequence silently mishandles indefinite-length and over-long TLVs
findings.body:
`readSequence()` does two unsafe things:
1. If `readLength()` returns -1 (BER indefinite-length encoding, which `readLength()` explicitly supports), the `while (length > 0)` test is false on entry and the method returns an empty list while leaving the end-of-contents marker and the entire sequence body unread. Callers will then see a zero-length list and either index out of bounds or silently accept an empty signature.
2. `readNext()` can in principle return more bytes than the declared remaining length (malformed input); in that case `length` underflows, the loop exits, and the leftover bytes are silently swallowed instead of being rejected as malformed.
The reader should either reject indefinite-length as not supported for DER or read until the 0x00 0x00 end-of-contents octets, and should validate that the consumed bytes never exceed the declared length.

findings.title: logger.debugf called with a plain string and no format arguments
findings.body: `logger.debugf(builder.toString());` passes a String with no `%` placeholders and no varargs to `debugf(String, Object...)`. This is misleading because the signature suggests a printf-style format string. If any discovered CryptoProvider class name ever contained a `%` (unlikely but not enforced), it would be interpreted as a format specifier and could throw. Use `logger.debug(builder.toString())` (or `logger.tracef` if formatting is desired) instead.

findings.title: Test uses a single P-256 key for ES256/ES384/ES512
findings.body: The constructor calls `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which on the standard SunEC provider returns a P-256 (secp256r1) key. That same key is then used to exercise ES256, ES384 and ES512, each of which expects a different curve and a different raw signature length (64, 96, 132 bytes respectively). With a P-256 key the SHA384withECDSA/SHA512withECDSA signatures still have only 32+32 byte components, so `getSignatureLength()` returns 96/132 while the real signature is 64 bytes; the test only round-trips the bytes through DER<->concatenatedRS and so happens to pass even though no ES384/ES512-shaped signature is ever produced. The test does not verify the conversion for genuinely larger curves and does not assert that a signature produced by `signature.sign()` round-trips to the original signature value for the expected length. Generate (or load) a key of the appropriate curve per algorithm and assert the round-tripped bytes actually equal the original `sign()` output.
